posts.text: Everyone is talking about becoming an AI Engineer in 2026. But there’s a problem. Most people are learning AI in the wrong order. They learn: → Prompt Engineering → ChatGPT → RAG → LangChain → LangGraph → MCP → AI Agents → Another 20 frameworks… And after months of learning, they still can't answer: “How do I build a production-ready AI Agent from scratch?” I’ve seen beginners struggle with this. And honestly, even experienced developers can get stuck here because the AI ecosystem is moving ridiculously fast. Every few weeks there is: A new model. A new agent framework. A new protocol. A new tool. A new tutorial. A new “roadmap.” So what should an Agentic AI Engineer in 2026 actually learn? Here’s the path I would follow: 01 — Python + Software Engineering Don't skip the fundamentals. APIs, async programming, Git, testing, databases, Docker and backend development. 02 — LLM Fundamentals Understand what you're actually working with. Tokens → Embeddings → Attention → Transformers → Context Windows → Inference → Model selection. 03 — Prompt Engineering Learn how to give models reliable instructions. Structured outputs, tool calling, few-shot prompting, reasoning patterns and prompt evaluation. 04 — RAG Teach your applications to work with private and changing knowledge. Chunking → Embeddings → Vector Search → Hybrid Search → Reranking → Query Rewriting → Evaluation. 05 — AI Agents This is where things get interesting. LLM + Tools + Memory + Planning + State + Orchestration. Build agents that don't just answer questions… but actually perform tasks. 06 — Agent Frameworks Learn frameworks after understanding the architecture. LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI and others. Don't become a framework operator. Become someone who understands why the framework exists. 07 — MCP + Agent Communication Learn how agents connect with external tools, data and services. 08 — Production AI This is where many tutorials stop. But real companies care about: → Evaluation → Observability → Guardrails → Security → Latency → Cost → Reliability → Human-in-the-loop → Monitoring → Failure recovery 09 — Build Real Projects Not another chatbot. Build: → AI Sales Agent → AI Customer Support Agent → AI Research Agent → AI Coding Agent → AI Operations Agent → Multi-Agent Business Workflow Then deploy it. Break it. Debug it. Measure it. Improve it. That's where the real learning happens. Want to become an Agentic AI Engineer in 2026? It may be the company with the best institutional memory. Models will continue to improve. They will also continue to change. That is the infrastructure layer I believe we are only beginning to appreciate. posts.text: I was pleased to be quoted by Taylor in this Digital IT News piece, but the more interesting part for me was reading everyone else’s answers. The article asks about the “best use” of enterprise AI. Read all of the responses together and a different question starts to emerge: What has to be true before enterprise AI can be trusted to matter? My answer is context. Enterprises already have extraordinary amounts of intelligence. But we have spent years breaking that intelligence apart. The conversation becomes a recording. The recording becomes a transcript. The transcript becomes a summary. The summary becomes a CRM note. Someone sends an email. Someone creates a task. Someone approves an exception. Then six months later, a human or AI agent is expected to understand why a decision was made. That is not primarily a model problem. It is a records problem. If AI gets the summary but loses the source, the evidence, the sequence, the promises, the qualifications, and what happened next, we should not be surprised when it confidently misunderstands the situation. This is why I keep coming back to the same conviction: AI needs better records. And as agents begin making more consequential decisions, context with provenance will matter a lot more than context alone.

posts.text: Annie Wang breaks down three foundational agent architectures in Google's Agent Development Kit: single, sequential, and parallel. A single agent handles straightforward tool execution, but complex multi-step tasks break down without coordination. Moving to a sequential pipeline gives you an assembly line where each stage validates its handoff, while parallel patterns let specialized workers fan out concurrently to cut latency. Architecture choices in multi-agent systems come down to where state lives and how handoffs are coordinated.

posts.text: I keep hearing “don’t automate the process, redesign the business around AI.” Sounds terrific from a conference stage, and sometimes it’s right. Automating a stupid process can just give you a faster stupid process. But redesign isn’t drawing some new boxes and a cleaner flow chart. Those boxes are people and the flow chart is how work actually gets done. Change it and you’re changing roles, systems, incentives, customer commitments and sometimes jobs while the business still has to carry on working. Sometimes you stop the work. Sometimes you automate it. Sometimes you redesign it. Sometimes automation is the redesign. I’m much more interested in the war stories from people who’ve actually had to make that transition work. posts.text: Responsible AI vs AI Governance 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗖𝗵𝗶𝗲𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿. 𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀. 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘄 → chiefaileader.com/pp Original post: __________ I still see Responsible AI and AI Governance being used almost interchangeably, even in job titles at some of the biggest firms. The definitions are not fully standardized, but a few credible sources provide enough clarity to distinguish between the two. So I took these sources and tried to find the common elements across them for both Responsible AI and AI Governance. And thankfully, there are some clear non-overlapping elements that make the distinction easier to understand. My personal favorite for Responsible AI is IAPP’s definition. It talks about “principle-based AI development.” Based on other definitions, I would simply extend that idea across the entire AI lifecycle: Principle-based AI design, development, deployment, use, monitoring, and governance. For AI Governance, again I find IAPP’s definition very comprehensive. It describes AI Governance as a system of frameworks, practices, and processes. I would extend that to: A system of frameworks, practices, processes, policies, tools, standards, controls, and guardrails that guide the implementation of Responsible AI. So, in a nutshell: Responsible AI tells us the principles and shows us what we should look after across the AI lifecycle. AI Governance gives us the system of (frameworks, practices, processes, policies, tools, standards, controls, and guardrails) to actually implement those principles and make Responsible AI happen in practice. There is definitely overlap, but they are not the same. Hope this helps clear up some of the confusion. Credit to Saahil Gupta, RAI. Follow him for more.

posts.text: Gartner said 30% of AI projects would be abandoned by 2025. Now it is mid 2026! Where are we? In August 2023, Gartner predicted that at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025. At the time, people called it pessimistic. Gartner was accused of not understanding the momentum. The prediction window closed. The data is in. McKinsey's 2026 State of AI report shows only 26% of AI initiatives reach production deployment. Bain's enterprise AI survey found 65% of POCs never advanced past pilot stage. Every CIO I've spoken to this year has a graveyard of AI experiments that looked promising in a demo and died when someone asked about integration, data quality, or who owns it after the consultants leave. 30% abandonment would have been a success story. The reality is closer to 50-70% 🔥 The pattern behind the failures is always the same: * The POC was built on clean sample data. Production data had edge cases, nulls, and definitions that changed quarterly. * The demo impressed a steering committee. Nobody asked who would maintain it, retrain it, or explain it when the output was wrong. * The project had executive sponsorship at kickoff. Six months later that executive had moved roles and the new one wanted their own initiative. None of these are technical failures. They are organisational failures wearing technical costumes. The companies that beat the odds share one trait: they treated AI projects like data projects, not like innovation theatre. They asked the boring questions early. Who owns the data this model depends on? Who owns the model after go-live? What happens when the output is wrong and a customer sees it? Gartner's prediction was not a warning about AI. It was a warning about how enterprises run projects. The technology worked. The organisations didn't. The 2027 prediction will be the same, unless the approach changes. posts.text: OpenAI just made the agent harness rentable. I am still polishing mine. The release changes my architecture, not my objective. The new Agents API puts the Codex harness behind an API. OpenAI manages long-running sessions, orchestration, context compaction, recovery and subagents. Developers provide the tools and choose the execution environment. That removes a large amount of infrastructure for teams whose advantage is domain knowledge or workflow design. But a harness also determines what happens when the happy path ends: → What survives when the context window fills? → What happens if a write succeeds but the session fails before recording it? → Which actions require approval, and where does the audit evidence live? These are product decisions once an agent can act on real systems. I learned this while testing context policy as a first-class design choice. In a scripted 40-fetch benchmark, a notes-and-search approach sent 66% fewer estimated prompt tokens than flat history while keeping all 40 tool results reachable. That is the shape of the effect, not a production benchmark. The policy still changed cost, continuity and behaviour. So my harness keeps identity, policy, approvals, budgets, audit and provider-neutral run state in the control plane. The agent runtime sits behind an adapter. Claude Code can be one runtime. The Agents API can be another. The choice is no longer whether to build or buy the entire harness. It is deciding what to rent and what must remain yours. A managed harness can remove infrastructure. It cannot decide which parts of agent behaviour you are willing to outsource. Video: OpenAI Developers

posts.text: Your company doesn’t need another AI pilot. It needs an AI operating model. I’ve seen organisations invest heavily in AI. The strategy looks impressive. The pilots are launched. The dashboards are built. The models perform well. And yet, six months later, the business is still asking the same questions. Why haven’t sales improved? Why are margins under pressure? Why is working capital still stuck? Why are supply-chain decisions still reactive? The problem is rarely the AI model. It is what happens around the model. AI creates value only when it becomes part of how the organisation actually operates. That means connecting AI to the processes where decisions are made sales, pricing, collections, demand planning, inventory, procurement, finance and customer operations. It means having trusted data underneath it. Clear ownership around it. People who know when to trust the recommendation and when to challenge it. And, most importantly, metrics that measure business outcomes, not technology activity. I would rather see an organisation move one AI capability into a critical business workflow and improve cash conversion by 5% than launch ten impressive pilots that never reach production. The real journey is not: Report → AI pilot → AI deployment It is: Data → Insight → Prediction → Decision → Action → Business outcome That is where the next phase of enterprise AI will be won. Not by the organisations that deploy the most models. But by the organisations that build the best operating model around them. The question for every CXO should no longer be, “Where can we use AI?” It should be: “Which business decision should AI help us make better, faster and more consistently?” That is where AI stops being a technology initiative and starts becoming a business capability. hashtag #ArtificialIntelligence hashtag #DigitalTransformation hashtag #EnterpriseAI hashtag #CIO hashtag #BusinessTransformation hashtag #DataStrategy hashtag #Leadership

posts.text: Open-source maintenance gets messy fast. This repo puts guardrails before AI agents. Hive is an open-source AI agent orchestration project for teams maintaining GitHub-based open-source projects. It helps you move issues and PRs through an agent workflow by classifying work before it reaches an LLM, then adjusting agent cadences to the queue depth. Key features: • GitHub work triage – enumerates issues and PRs, then classifies them by complexity • Deterministic pipeline – handles filtering, classification, merge-gating, and enforcement before agent judgment calls • Multiple agent backends – supports Claude, Copilot, Gemini, and Goose for code-reading, fixes, and PR work • Queue-aware governor – switches between surge, busy, quiet, and idle modes with different agent cadences • Configurable autonomy – ACMM levels define whether agents advise, file issues, open hold-gated PRs, or auto-merge on green CI It’s open-source (Apache License 2.0). 🔗 GitHub: https://lnkd.in/dnWKmA-t ⸻ ♻️ Share this with your network if you found it useful or insightful. ✉️ If you’re into AI, ML, agents, and building real systems, join my newsletter (it’s free): dankornas.substack.com

posts.text: Three years ago, most enterprise AI was experienced as a prompt, a chat reply, one model and an API call. Look at what a builder can reach for today: one model that reads text, images, audio, video and whole documents, with a context window past a million tokens the ability to call tools, search, run code and operate software directly work that continues across many steps, choosing models and depth of reasoning as it goes For selected models, the price of a million tokens has fallen from tens of dollars to cents, even as the cost of dependable work has not. The materials for building enterprise AI have genuinely changed. But materials are not systems. AI can connect to enterprise systems more readily than it can be given safe authority, continue through many steps more readily than finish the whole task dependably, and record what happened more readily than say who is accountable. Mindvista Edition 78 maps these new materials and, harder, their maturity: what is ready to use, what to pilot, what to explore through POCs, and what is still unproven or overstated. The advances are real. The experience and value built on them lag behind. This is the beginning of a Second Age for builders. What each of us assembles from these materials, for whom, and to what human purpose, will decide whether the enterprise ever truly enters it. 1.Do you see these as the beginning of a Second Age of enterprise AI, and which materials matter most? 2.Where does your experience place their maturity: ready to use, pilot, explore, or still overstated? 3.What has helped or challenged your own transition? Love to hear your reactions, experiences and perspectives. posts.text: There are two bad approaches to AI governance. One is unrestricted experimentation. The other is making every AI idea survive a six-month approval process. Neither scales. Good governance should be proportional to risk. A low-risk productivity use case should not require the same scrutiny as an AI system influencing hiring, financial, healthcare, legal, or security decisions. That’s the leadership challenge: create enough structure to protect the business without making responsible innovation impossible. Start with three things: • Know what AI is already being used. • Establish clear ownership. • Classify use cases by business and data risk. Then give teams a predictable process for getting appropriate use cases approved. Governance isn’t about saying “no” to AI. It’s about making better “yes” decisions. Our latest guide walks through practical AI governance frameworks and best practices. hashtag #AILeadership hashtag #Governance hashtag #EnterpriseAI hashtag #RiskManagement https://lnkd.in/gRknM7CE

posts.text: Generative AI has solved the problem of scale, but it has introduced a far more dangerous threat for brands: a rapid descent into the “statistical middle.” When every company has access to the same generative tools, the inevitable result is a sea of homogeneous, average content. AI orchestration and automated media planning and buying are critical, they are the modern plumbing. But the only way to escape the statistical middle is through exceptional human creativity, cultural insight, and strategic taste. Technology is the enabler; the human brain is the differentiator. posts.author: Suresh Rajashekaraiah • 2nd
posts.text: AI transformation is not primarily a technology transformation. It is an operating model transformation. Many enterprises begin with models, copilots and agents. But the real shift happens when AI changes how work is executed, who decides and how governance operates. Deploying AI without redesigning the operating model often creates limited value: faster tasks, but the same bottlenecks, approval chains, silos and governance friction. The deeper shift is from: Human executes. System supports. to: Human governs. AI executes within defined boundaries. This changes the enterprise itself. 1. Work becomes human + agent work AI agents can retrieve context, reason, invoke tools, coordinate workflows, validate outcomes and escalate exceptions. Work must be redesigned around people and digital actors. 2. Decision rights become an architecture concern The question is not only “Which model should we use?” It is “Who is authorized to make which decision?” Enterprises need explicit boundaries across Recommend, Assist, Execute, Decide and Govern. 3. Governance moves into the execution path Manual review boards cannot scale to millions of AI-driven actions. Policies, risk thresholds, security controls and approval rules must become machine-enforceable through Policy-as-Code, Architecture-as-Code and Decision-Rights-as-Code. 4. Roles evolve Architects, engineers, SREs and product owners will spend less time on repetitive execution and more time defining intent, guardrails, policies, exceptions and outcomes. 5. Autonomy becomes a managed variable Not every process should be autonomous. Enterprises need levels from manual execution to assist, recommend, act-with-approval and bounded autonomy. The level should depend on risk and blast radius. 6. Enterprise Architecture becomes more important AI introduces models, agents, tools, memory, knowledge and platforms. Without discipline, organizations risk agent sprawl, duplicated capabilities and rising cost. Transformation should start with business outcomes, capabilities, value streams and decision architecture before jumping to AI platforms. A strong AI operating model connects: Strategy → Capabilities → Decisions → Human/Agent Responsibilities → Governance → Data → Platforms → Automation → Observability → Continuous Improvement. The goal is not to deploy the maximum number of agents. The goal is to create a more adaptive enterprise where humans retain accountability while AI accelerates execution safely and economically. The strategic question is no longer: “Where can we use AI?” It is: “How should our enterprise operate when intelligent agents become participants in work, decisions and execution?” That is AI transformation. hashtag #AI hashtag #AINative hashtag #AIEngineering hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #GenAI hashtag #AIReasoning hashtag #EnterpriseArchitecture hashtag #OperatingModel hashtag #DigitalTransformation hashtag #AIGovernance hashtag #Automation hashtag #AgentOps hashtag #EngineeringLeadership hashtag #AITransformation hashtag #FutureReady hashtag #AIReadiness

posts.text: Most AI automation projects do not fail because the model is weak. They fail because the process was never stable to begin with. If a workflow has unclear ownership, inconsistent inputs, undocumented exceptions, and no baseline metric, AI will not “fix” it. It will automate confusion at a higher speed. Before introducing an agent, I would ask: -What decision is being made repeatedly? -What inputs are required? -Which exceptions still need human judgment? -What metric should improve: cycle time, SLA adherence, quality, or cost? AI works best when it sits on top of a process that is already visible, measurable, and owned. The goal is not to automate everything. The goal is to remove friction without removing accountability. What is one process in your organization that looks ready for AI—but actually needs process redesign first? hashtag #AITransformation hashtag #Operations hashtag #ProcessImprovement
